items.title: L’ora di plastica
items.summary: Di solito questo materiale non compare nei programmi di scuola, ma negli Stati Uniti è diventato una materia d’insegnamento Leggi
items.content:
Negli Stati Uniti, dove le lezioni sono ricominciate per circa 54 milioni di bambine e ragazzi, tra le materie insegnate in classe ce n’è una che non compare nei programmi: la plastica. Un rapporto della ong Plastic pollution coalition documenta come da anni l’industria del settore s’infiltra nelle scuole statunitensi con schede didattiche , video intitolati “La tua bottiglia significa posti di lavoro”, esperimenti pratici o giochi.

C’è perfino un furgone, il PlastiVan, che gira le città per raccontare “il contributo della plastica alla vita moderna”: secondo la Society of plastics engineers, l’associazione che lo paga (legata ai produttori), avrebbe raggiunto più di 132mila studenti.

Tutte queste proposte e materiali insistono su quanto la plastica sia sicura e indispensabile, minimizzando i rischi per la salute e l’ambiente. Un programma per le classi delle elementari e delle medie finanziato dalla Dow Chemical (una delle più grandi multinazionali chimiche al mondo) insegna agli alunni come testare i sacchetti di plastica di varie marche e poi gli chiede di fingersi dipendenti della Dow e progettarne uno.

Questi metodi sono più frequenti vicino agli impianti petrolchimici: in Pennsylvania, dove gestisce un complesso da 156 ettari per la produzione di plastica, la Shell ha proposto moduli didattici e donato zaini e un campo da basket a una scuola del posto ottenendo in cambio che nel programma si insegni la raccolta differenziata per il riciclo della plastica.

A volte durante le attività si riconosce che l’inquinamento da plastica è un problema grave, spiega Grist, una rivista dedicata al cambiamento climatico. Ma la responsabilità si fa ricadere sempre sui comportamenti individuali, indicando appunto la raccolta differenziata come soluzione (nel mondo si ricicla solo il 9 per cento della plastica prodotta).

Interpellata da Grist, Wendy Johnson, del National center for science education, aggiunge un altro grosso limite pedagogico: nei materiali didattici è scritto che sono in linea con gli standard per le discipline stem (matematica, fisica, chimica, biologia, informatica, tecnologia), ma non si specifica quali standard né in che modo siano rispettati. E si usano termini tecnici che danno l’illusione di rigore scientifico quando invece servono solo a veicolare l’idea che abbiamo bisogno di cose a basso costo.

Il rapporto riconosce tuttavia che, soprattutto per le materie stem, spesso gli insegnanti non hanno il tempo né le risorse per preparare le loro lezioni o comprare i materiali per i laboratori in classe o i progetti scientifici. Per questo quando un settore produttivo – anche molto discusso, come l’industria del tabacco , del cibo spazzatura , dei pesticidi o dei combustibili fossili – offre il suo aiuto gratuitamente o a prezzi bassissimi può essere difficile dire di no.

Come uscirne? Se la Plastic pollution coalition chiede ai consigli scolastici di vietare i programmi sponsorizzati, altre ong restano titubanti sui divieti generalizzati, preferendo fidarsi della capacità critica di insegnanti ed educatrici.

Sulla questione delle risorse che mancano, una strada può essere eliminare le agevolazioni fiscali per gli impianti che producono plastica, indirizzando i ricavi verso le scuole, suggerisce Grist.

Ci sono comunque delle alternative, sviluppate da realtà senza interessi di parte, per parlare a ragazze e ragazzi dell’inquinamento o dei costi e delle conseguenze dei processi con cui si fabbrica quello che consumiamo. E resta l’inventiva delle insegnanti, come una maestra di una scuola primaria in California che da undici anni trasforma la sua aula in un laboratorio a rifiuti zero.

Internazionale pubblica ogni settimana una pagina di lettere. Ci piacerebbe sapere cosa pensi di questo articolo. Scrivici a: posta@internazionale.it

items.title: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis
items.summary: More than 50 protests took place on Saturday after the government failed to get emergency legislation through parliament.
items.content:
Tens of thousands of people have protested across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation.

About 50 marches took place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona.

"There is a lot of anger in the streets," a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union said. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city.

The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase.

Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property.

Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.

His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament.

Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87

Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, which was hosting a real estate summit.

Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported. Public broadcaster RTVE said nine police officers were injured and five people were arrested.

One of the biggest demonstration happened in the capital, Madrid, where estimates of the number of participants varied widely. The city's Tenants' Union said there were 500,000, while officials put the figure at 70,000.

Demonstrators held banners reading "There won't be peace for rentism" and "I study to have a future, not to have a tiny apartment". They shook the keys they were holding and chanted: "We have the keys of all the city".

Some had also camped in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days.

One protester, David, told RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction."

Another protester, 26-year-old librarian Marcos Sainz, told AFP news agency that he used to share a two-bedroom flat with friends, paying 900 euros (£766) a month in rent. Today, he said a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros.

Sainz said he would protest against rent rises "until someone dares to regulate it all", or "we'll all have to leave Madrid".

Spanish police said they had arrested three members of a far-right group, some of whom had performed Nazi salutes, as they tried to reach demonstrators in the square.

On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives".

The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two decrees.

The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds".

The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union.

MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.

Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.

However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.

Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.

The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.

Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage

The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.

House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.

The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents.

It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively.

items.title: We're working on a new RuneScape MMO
items.summary: Article URL: https://play.runescape.com/4 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49949588 Points: 52 # Comments: 17
items.content:
At RuneFest, we gave you the first glimpse of something we’ve been quietly working on: an entirely new RuneScape MMORPG, built in Unreal Engine and set in the world of Gielinor.

Right now, it’s rocking a working title: RS4. That isn't necessarily the name we’ll eventually settle on, but this is our fourth generation RuneScape project, so RS4 works pretty well for now.

We thought long and hard about revealing this project so early. We could have kept it behind closed doors for much longer, especially given that we are still right at the beginning of a hugely ambitious project and the game is still a few years away. But ultimately, that didn't feel very RuneScape, or very us. For 25 years, RuneScape has been shaped by its players. We've learned that our games are at their best when we build with you, not just for you. So we want to do that from the beginning, and that means bringing you into the development journey earlier than you might expect - sharing ideas, testing things, listening and learning as we go. We want to build on the best of the tech development we've learned on Dragonwilds, and the best of the community co-development we've learned through RuneScape and Old School, and apply those principles to something new. And of course, as a RuneScape game, integrity and permanent progression will be central to our design principles.

Let's make one thing really clear. RS4 is not a replacement for any of our games, be it Old School, RuneScape or Dragonwilds. Those games have their own dedicated teams, exciting roadmaps and continued investment. We’ll be designing RS4 to sit alongside them as an additional way to experience RuneScape and the world of Gielinor. In fact, we think having different RuneScape experiences can make the whole family stronger. Players may spend most of their time in one game, move between several, or discover Gielinor for the very first time through RS4. The ambition isn't to replace the RuneScape games you love. It's to make the RuneScape universe bigger.

RS4 will be set in Gielinor, in the Sixth Age. But we're beginning somewhere that RuneScape players have only recently started to discover - and that is Ashenfall. An area first explored in RuneScape: Dragonwilds, and a landmass to the north-east of the Gielinor. RS4 will take place years after the events of Dragonwilds and the destruction of the Dragon Queen Kuldra. Time has passed, the world has moved on, and Ashenfall has changed with it. But Ashenfall is only the beginning. Our ambition is for this adventure to grow far beyond Ashenfall over time, moving into places you know and love, as well as opening up new places and stories across Gielinor.

We know our incredible community and that means we’re sure you have a million questions. Which platforms? What accounts? Membership? Progression? Combat? Skills? When can you actually play it? But, the answer right now is that it's simply not the right time, or just too early, for us to say. This isn't the full reveal – more an opportunity for us to share the beginning of something special with you. We'll tell you much more next year about the world, the game, the team building it and, importantly, how you can start getting involved. For now, there are a few things we want you to know:

It sits alongside RuneScape, Old School RuneScape and Dragonwilds as an independent experience

It will be true to our principles of integrity, permanent progression, and community driven development

It's still a few years away, but we're telling you now because we want to build it with you.

25 years ago, RuneScape began with a world, a small team and a community that helped turn it into something far bigger than anyone could have imagined. Now we get to start another adventure together.

items.title: We're going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything
items.summary: Article URL: https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/3/default-hard-budget-caps/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49949235 Points: 406 # Comments: 203
items.content:
Here’s a product feature which the world is going to need a whole lot more of over the coming months and years: default hard budget caps . I’m talking about the feature of pay-by-usage services and APIs that lets you say “after $X/month, cut this thing off and return errors”. These need to be hard limits. Soft caps, “after $X/month, send me a warning email”, will not cut it.

Coding agents, and personal agents (coding agents wrapped in a less threatening UI), greatly reduce the friction of spinning up code that can do useful things. Sometimes those things cost money—calls to paid APIs, or hosted web applications, or systems that can bill for additional storage and compute.

Nobody wants to wake up to an email sent at midnight warning about a budget limit and find that, while they slept, their rogue service had consumed several hundred (or several thousand) more dollars of usage.

An argument against this is that businesses don’t want their hosted applications to start throwing errors because some budget was exceeded. I expect that most businesses and individuals would prefer errors to a surprise $10,000+ bill.

I think hard budget caps need to be the default. If someone wants to live dangerously they should be able to do that, but it needs to be on an opt-in basis. Have a nice, clear checkbox somewhere prominent:

Remove the budget cap. My application will not be shut down if I exceed the configured budget limit, and I will be responsible for subsequent charges.

The service I most want to see this from is AWS. I’ve heard plenty of stories from people who refuse to use AWS for personal projects out of (justified) fear that a runaway service might bankrupt them. I’ve also heard stories from people who didn’t anticipate this and ended up seriously burned.

... and it turns out AWS finally launched spending limits a few weeks ago! From their announcement New AWS experience helps builders get started and ship faster on 16th September:

When you’re ready to upgrade to a paid plan, you can set a monthly spend limit for your project based on your usage patterns so that you stay within your budget. If a project’s usage reaches its spend limit, your project is paused for that month.

See also Create a spend limit in AWS Settings , though that page warns that “We’re currently releasing our new experience to a limited number of customers.” Here’s hoping that hits general availability for existing accounts soon.

Google Cloud launched a similar feature in July, called Spend Caps, which lets you “set a monthly financial cap on specific services within a project”. Looks like this is becoming a trend!

In an ideal world, our agents could help with this. It would be great if agents started biasing towards recommending providers with hard budget caps, and warning new and inexperienced builders against deploying applications using uncapped services that might get them into trouble.

This is We’re going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything by Simon Willison, posted on 3rd October 2026 .

items.title: Cornell president says university 'must do better' after frat house rape allegations
items.summary: Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations of a woman who says she was drugged and gang raped as "deeply disturbing".
items.content:
Cornell University's president says the school "must do better" after a woman alleged she was drugged and raped by a group of men at a fraternity house.

In an eight-minute video statement released on Saturday night, Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations raised by the woman, identified as Jane Doe, as "deeply disturbing".

The alleged incident has raised questions around the culture on campus of drug and alcohol use, and the way investigations were conducted in the case, Kotlikoff said.

Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the university when she says seven men from its Chi Phi fraternity assaulted her for hours in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine on 19 October 2024.

She said she had reported the incident two weeks after it happened to Cornell University police, which investigated, but no charges were laid.

Last month, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university, in which she alleged Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved.

Kotlikoff said Cornell was "committed to investigating" the way the case was handled, and said the school administration and community "must do better".

"We must foster a culture in which sexual assault is inexcusable and ensure our community is empowered and understands informed consent," he said.

He added that university leaders need to create an environment where victims of sexual assault "feel safe coming forward and are treated with compassion and dignity".

Kotlikoff said it is a "defining moment" in the university's history.

"We must lead the way, we owe it to Jane Doe and to survivors of assault to get this right. And we must keep each other safe," he said.

On the university's campus this week, the BBC saw growing frustration about the situation.

At a public hearing for students to speak about the alleged gang rape, many told the BBC they were ashamed of what happened and said the university had failed Jane Doe.

"Our administration needs to change and it needs to change drastically and it needs to change fast," one student told the BBC. "Something like this never should have happened, this is a disgrace."

As part of "broader work" that needs to happen, Kotlikoff said in his video statement that there should be a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life".

"Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others, or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said.

The university president also said that at the "appropriate time", the school would speak about how Cornell will "use this moment, this conversation, this anger, to help lead the broader effort to combat sexual assault not only on our campus, but beyond it".

New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled, and has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead a review of the case.

Kotlikoff said he supported the decision to appoint James to lead a criminal investigation, and welcomed an independent review by a law firm of how Cornell has handled the matter.

Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and could not provide consent.

items.title: Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
items.summary: Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
items.content:
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.

Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.

Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.

On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.

Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.

The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.

But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.

Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.

The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.

Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.

"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.

Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.

We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.

Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.

"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.

Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.

One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.

''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''

In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.

But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world , external , others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.

Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.

"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.

Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.

"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.

"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.

For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.

"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."

Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.

Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.

But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.

Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.

The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.

He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.

"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.

For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

items.title: Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion
items.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the military is running scenarios in the unlikely case the US invades Canada.
items.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.

Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency.

Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.

In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims.

"President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.

Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.

In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.

A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions.

"I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.

Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.

They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.

The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.

Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.

After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.

But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum.

"Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.

Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.

Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.

In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.

Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.

Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.

It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.

They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.

A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared.

"That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."

Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.

He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.

"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.

Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.

According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week

Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.

Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.

The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.

The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.

He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.

Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.

An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.

Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.

"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.

Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.

But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.

"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.

Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

items.title: US father and son arrested after 'gas station heroin' deaths
items.summary: They are accused of selling at least one student derivatives of kratom, often called "gas station heroin" in the US.
items.content:
A father and son who worked at a Mississippi smoke shop have been arrested and charged in connection with the death of at least one university student who died from a suspected overdose of kratom, sometimes called "gas station heroin" in the US.

The pair worked at a shop that allegedly sold derivatives of the substance to University of Mississippi students.

US prosecutors charged Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Yahya Mosleh, 18, for possession with the intent to distribute controlled substances in connection with the death investigation of two Ole Miss students last month.

Although their deaths have not officially been attributed to kratom, officials afterward issued warnings about consuming kratom .

The criminal complaint alleges that on 21 September, an Ole Miss student was found dead in his dorm room. The apparent cause of death "appeared to be consistent with a drug overdose", the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Mississippi said in a press release.

Law enforcement found packages - with some tablets missing - of suspected kratom derivatives.

About an hour later, a second student was found dead from a suspected overdose in another location, also with packages of suspected kratom derivatives.

Officials connected the packages with the local vape, tobacco and beer store, the US Attorney's statement said.

Law enforcement executed search warrants and seized suspected kratom derivative controlled substances from the store. The Mosleh's, father and son, were later arrested.

The two students' deaths have sparked alarm and warnings from officials about the plant-based drug referred to as "gas station heroin".

Kratom - a herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over the counter and consumed in pill or liquid form.

For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it is illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi.

The Mississippi prosecutors said that kratom derivatives, such as MGPI, MGM-15 and MGM-16, are now schedule I controlled substances in the US and can be significantly more potent than natural kratom leaf products and morphine.

What is kratom, the 'gas station heroin' alarming officials in the US?

items.title: Guerra in Iran, le news di oggi. Trump: “Stato iraniano decimato, devo decidere se usare linea dura”
items.summary: Teheran: “Arrivata una proposta dagli Usa”. Hegseth: “Blocco a Hormuz è ferreo”
items.content:
"Prenderò una decisione riguardo all'Iran. È stato decimato. L'unica domanda è se si sceglie la via facile o la linea dura", ha affermato il presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump . Duro anche Hegseth : “Il blocco a Hormuz è ferreo”. Ma da Teheran fanno sapere che gli Usa avrebbero mandato una nuova proposta.

Netanyahu: “Il copilota di Flydubai islamista radicalizzato”

La pista del jihadista solitario. “Sventato nuovo 11 settembre”

Flydubai: chi può aprire la porta della cabina di pilotaggio e perché solo in un caso è impossibile

Ucciso in un raid dell’Idf a Gaza il direttore di una ong umanitaria turca

Il direttore nella Striscia di Gaza dell'organizzazione umanitaria turca Deniz Feneri, Saqer al Qaisi, è stato ucciso questa mattina in un attacco israeliano contro un veicolo a Deir al Balah, nel centro dell'enclave. Lo riferiscono i servizi di ambulanza ed emergenza gazawi, secondo cui altre dieci persone sono rimaste ferite. L'identità della vittima è stata confermata dall'ospedale dei Martiri di Al Aqsa, che ne ha ricevuto il corpo. Interpellato da Efe , l'esercito israeliano ha dichiarato che il raid aveva come obiettivo un membro di Hamas, senza precisare se si trattasse di Al Qaisi né fornire dettagli su suoi eventuali legami con il movimento. Secondo l'agenzia ufficiale palestinese Wafa , è morta oggi anche Suha Nasser, una bambina di sei anni ferita due settimane fa da colpi d'arma da fuoco che avevano raggiunto la sua tenda. Nel nord della Striscia, a Beit Lahia, altre quattro persone sono rimaste ferite in un attacco aereo israeliano, riferisce l'ospedale Shifa di Gaza. Il ministero della Sanità gazawi afferma che oltre 1.400 persone sono state uccise dalle forze israeliane dall'entrata in vigore del cessate il fuoco nell'ottobre 2025. Il bilancio complessivo dei morti dal 7 ottobre 2023 supera quota 74.228, secondo la stessa fonte.

Teheran: “Gli Usa vogliono parlare di nucleare, noi di Hormuz”

"Così come prendiamo sul serio l'autodifesa, siamo altrettanto fermi e risoluti sia nel difendere noi stessi sia nel portare avanti la diplomazia": è quanto dichiarato oggi dal ministro degli Esteri iraniano, Abbas Araghchi, citato dall'agenzia Irna . "Se i nostri avversari dovessero scegliere ancora una volta la via dello scontro militare — ha proseguito — si troveranno ad affrontare una risposta molto più dura di quelle precedenti. Tuttavia, se intendono perseguire la via diplomatica, siamo pronti a raggiungere attraverso la diplomazia una soluzione equa e dignitosa per porre fine a questo conflitto". In merito al nuovo piano dell'Iran per risolvere le controversie ancora in corso con gli Stati Uniti, Araghchi ha sottolineato che, se gli Stati Uniti accetteranno il piano iraniano di sette giorni, lo Stretto di Hormuz verrà riaperto entro i sette giorni.

Una nave cisterna ha segnalato di essere stata colpita da un proiettile non identificato nello Stretto di Hormuz, riportando danni alla sala macchine. Lo riferisce l'autorità marittima britannica, citata da Al Arabiya. I membri dell'equipaggio sono al sicuro e non risultano segnalazioni di conseguenze ambientali.

Araghchi: “Non c'è soluzione militare alla guerra, ma solo col negoziato”

“Non esiste una soluzione militare, né una soluzione basata su ulteriori sanzioni; solo un approccio fondato sul negoziato, sull'equità e sulla dignità diplomatica può offrire una soluzione definitiva a questa guerra”. Lo ha detto il ministro degli esteri dell'Iran, Abbas Araghchi , parlando del conflitto con gli Usa. “Gli Stati Uniti hanno già fallito in passato sia sul piano militare che su quello diplomatico, ma tentare la strada delle sanzioni, incluse quelle nuove, non porterà loro alcun beneficio”, ha aggiunto, sottolineando: “Ci auguriamo che gli Stati Uniti scelgano la via della saggezza e della razionalità”.

Gli Stati Uniti hanno recentemente trasmesso proposte all'Iran attraverso intermediari, pur sostenendo una posizione diversa sui media. Lo ha dichiarato il presidente del Parlamento iraniano e capo negoziatore, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf , secondo quanto riporta Al Jazeera. "Washington deve rendersi conto che la fase in cui si prende tempo e si impongono richieste unilaterali è finita", ha aggiunto. Il presidente del Parlamento ha inoltre ribadito le condizioni di Teheran per la riapertura dello Stretto di Hormuz: "Le nostre posizioni sono chiare e lo Stretto non sarà riaperto finché non saranno soddisfatte le nostre sette condizioni, conformemente al memorandum d'intesa".

Media, l'esercito iraniano fornirà un addestramento militare di base ai civili

L'esercito iraniano ha in programma di avviare l'addestramento di volontari nell'ambito di un programma volto a preparare i cittadini alla "difesa nazionale", secondo quanto riferito dall'agenzia di stampa iraniana West Asia News Agency (Wana) e riportato da Al Jazeera. Il generale di brigata Mohammad Reza Alian-Nejad , responsabile dell'addestramento e della formazione dell'esercito, ha dichiarato che il programma si svolgerà a partire da oggi presso tre strutture a Teheran. Alian-Nejad ha affermato che il personale proveniente dalle quattro branche dell'esercito sarà dislocato in diverse sedi designate come "presidi campali" per fornire ai volontari un "addestramento militare di base", seguito da corsi più avanzati.

Le autorità giordane hanno arrestato un diciottenne sospettato di appartenere a ShinyHunters, il gruppo di criminali informatici che ha rivendicato un furto di dati ai danni dell'Fbi. Lo riferisce la televisione pubblica Al Mamlaka, citando una fonte ufficiale giordana. Il giovane, cittadino giordano, è stato fermato la scorsa settimana. Sono in corso accertamenti sulle attività del gruppo e sulle organizzazioni a esso collegate, ha aggiunto la fonte, senza fornire ulteriori dettagli.

Procura portoghese apre indagine su concessione base Lajes a Usa

La procura portoghese ha aperto un'indagine sulla legittimità dell'autorizzazione concessa dal governo di Lisbona agli Stati Uniti per utilizzare la base aerea di Lajes, nelle Azzorre, durante la guerra con l'Iran. Lo ha reso noto la Procura generale portoghese, precisando che l'inchiesta è stata avviata in seguito a una denuncia presentata da esponenti del partito di sinistra Bloco de Esquerda. Il governo di centrodestra aveva autorizzato a marzo diversi voli di transito statunitensi attraverso la base, suscitando le critiche dei partiti di opposizione di sinistra.

Iran: arrestati 31 sospetti, smantellate 4 reti di sabotaggio legate a Usa e Israele

Le autorità iraniane hanno arrestato 31 persone accusate di appartenere a quattro reti sostenute da Stati Uniti e Israele e coinvolte in piani per fomentare disordini e compiere atti di sabotaggio nella provincia meridionale di Kerman. Lo ha reso noto il ministero dell'Intelligence iraniano, citato da Press Tv. Secondo Teheran, i sospetti operavano nella contea di Sirjan e avrebbero cercato di "adescare adolescenti e giovani", preparando inoltre "grandi quantità di molotov" da utilizzare per danneggiare le telecamere di sorveglianza urbana in vista di "disordini di strada e atti di sabotaggio".

Attacco aereo saudita sullo Yemen, esplosioni vicino l'aeroporto di Riad

Gli aerei da guerra sauditi hanno preso di mira la città di Abs, nella provincia di Hajjah, nello Yemen, secondo quanto riporta l'agenzia iraniana Tasnim. Poche ore prima, diverse fonti arabe della regione hanno riferito di esplosioni a Buqayq, in Arabia Saudita, a seguito di un attacco con missili balistici da parte delle forze yemenite. Fonti della regione poi hanno segnalato forti esplosioni anche nei pressi dell'aeroporto di Riad.

La Russia è pronta a svolgere un ruolo di mediazione tra Stati Uniti e Iran per contribuire a porre fine alla guerra e non sacrificherà i propri rapporti con Teheran. Lo ha dichiarato il vicepresidente del Consiglio di sicurezza russo Dmitry Medvedev ai media iraniani, sottolineando che le relazioni tra Mosca e Teheran hanno raggiunto "un livello senza precedenti" e che nell'ultimo anno gli scambi commerciali bilaterali sono aumentati del 20%. Russia e Iran, ha aggiunto, sono sottoposti a "sanzioni su vasta scala" e devono quindi sviluppare meccanismi alternativi di cooperazione finanziaria, ricordando che circa il 90% degli scambi tra i Paesi dell'Organizzazione per la cooperazione di Shanghai avviene ormai nelle rispettive valute nazionali.

Hegseth: “Blocco a Hormuz è ferreo, Trump ha tutte opzioni sul tavolo”

"Il nostro blocco è ferreo". Lo ha dichiarato il segretario alla Difesa americano Pete Hegseth, assicurando che gli Stati Uniti mantengono il controllo dello Stretto di Hormuz e avvertendo Teheran delle possibili conseguenze se continuerà a "giocare" con il passaggio marittimo strategico. "L'Iran vuole giocare con cose come lo Stretto di Hormuz. Non lo controllano loro, lo controlliamo noi. Non sono riusciti a far passare letteralmente nulla", ha affermato Hegseth, invitando Teheran a "fare la scelta giusta". "Se non lo farà, il presidente avrà sul tavolo tutte le opzioni di cui ha bisogno. Ma non lascerà che questa situazione si prolunghi inutilmente. Sa qual è la missione e, quando ci verrà chiesto, siamo in grado di portarla a termine", ha aggiunto.

items.title: Guerra Ucraina - Russia, le news di oggi. Colpito il Ponte Nord in pieno giorno mentre Merz è a Kiev
items.summary: La visita a sorpresa del cancelliere tedesco. Onu: “Oltre 15mila civili uccisi o feriti nel 2026”. Rapporto shock sugli stupri
items.content:
Nei primi otto mesi del 2026 in Ucraina si sono registrati in media oltre 400 civili uccisi o feriti ogni settimana, con un aumento del 55% rispetto allo stesso periodo del 2025. Lo ha dichiarato l'Alto commissario delle Nazioni Unite per i Diritti Umani Volker Turk al Consiglio per i diritti umani a Ginevra. L'ufficio ha inoltre riscontrato livelli "scioccanti" di violenza sessuale contro civili e prigionieri di guerra. Merz intanto a Kiev per una visita a sorpresa, udite esplosioni nella capitale

Colpito nuovamente il Ponte Nord di Kiev durante visita Merz

"Ci saranno importanti accordi tra Ucraina e Germania". Lo annuncia su X il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky , in occasione della visita a Kiev del cancelliere tedesco Friedrich Merz. "Oggi prepariamo decisioni che daranno a noi in Ucraina e a tutta l'Europa maggiori capacità di difenderci", scrive Zelensky, ringraziando la Germania per il sostegno e per il ruolo svolto nella protezione delle vite degli ucraini dagli attacchi russi. "La Russia deve essere fermata insieme. Grazie a tutti coloro che ci aiutano", conclude.

This morning, the Russians once again struck the Pivnichnyi Bridge in Kyiv with a drone. They attacked an ordinary pharmaceutical warehouse in Sumy with drones. Tragically, one person was killed. My condolences to the family and loved ones. In Dnipro, they struck a communications facility. Six people were injured as a result of these attacks. Overnight, the Russians launched 135 attack drones against Ukraine, more than 50 of them jet-powered. Kyiv, the Dnipro, Kharkiv, Donetsk, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia regions came under attack. And among the main targets of these terrorists, as always, are ordinary residential buildings, critical infrastructure – everything that makes up normal everyday life. There are power outages in some communities. Our services are working at the impact sites. It is important that Ukraine is not left alone against this terror. This week alone, the Russians have used more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 25 missiles against Ukraine. More than 800 of the drones were jet-powered, and Russia must be held accountable for this escalation. Today, Friedrich Merz @bundeskanzler – Federal Chancellor of Germany – is visiting Kyiv. A leader of a country that consistently demonstrates leadership in protecting the lives of Ukrainians from Russian strikes. We are grateful for all the support, and today we are preparing decisions to give us in Ukraine, and all of Europe, greater capabilities to defend ourselves. There will be important agreements between Ukraine and Germany. Russia must be stopped together. Thank you to everyone who is helping.

Colpito nuovamente il Ponte Nord di Kiev durante visita Merz

Il Ponte Nord di Kiev è stato nuovamente colpito dalla Russia. Lo riferisce il sindaco della capitale ucraina Vitali Klitschko sul suo canale Telegram, aggiungendo che "i servizi di emergenza sono in arrivo sul posto". È in corso nella capitale Ucraina la visita del cancelliere tedesco Friedrich Merz. Anche ieri un drone russo aveva colpito il ponte che collega le due sponde del fiume Dnipro.

Video captures the moment a Russian strike directly hit civilian vehicles crossing Kyiv’s North Bridge in broad daylight. The blast tore through daytime traffic on the major thoroughfare, damaging multiple cars and severing transit links. Video: Telegram channels pic.twitter.com/oBdVqB7qhd

Esplosioni sono state avvertite a Kiev mentre prende il via la visita del cancelliere tedesco Friedrich Merz nella capitale ucraina. Le deflagrazioni sono state precedute dalle sirene d'allarme aereo e da un avviso sulla presenza di droni russi nello spazio aereo.

Merz annuncerà misure da 1 miliardo di euro in aiuti militari e 350 milioni per energia

Merz annuncerà un pacchetto di misure che prevede lo stanziamento di un miliardo di euro in aiuti militari e 350 milioni di euro per interventi nel settore energetico. Lo scrive Reuters sul suo sito citando funzionari del governo tedesco. È inoltre previsto che durante la visita venga finalizzato un accordo per la produzione congiunta di diverse tipologie di droni. Il cancelliere tedesco è accompagnato anche da una delegazione economica che comprende dirigenti di Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence, Quantum Systems e altre aziende. Si prevede inoltre che Merz solleciti il governo ucraino a compiere progressi sulle riforme richieste dai partner dell'Ue, compresa la lotta alla corruzione.

Merz: “Anche la sicurezza della Germania dipende dall’esito della guerra”

"L'Ucraina si trova davanti a settimane decisive. Per questo motivo sono oggi partito per Kiev con il messaggio: potete contare su di noi. Anche la sicurezza della Germania dipende dall'esito di questa guerra. Per questo motivo aiutiamo anche per interesse nostro proprio". Lo scrive su X il cancelliere tedesco, Friedrich Merz , oggi in visita nel Paese.

Il cancelliere tedesco Friedrich Merz è arrivato a Kiev, accompagnato dagli amministratori delegati di aziende tedesche del settore della difesa, per dimostrare il proprio sostegno al presidente Volodymyr Zelenskiy in un contesto di crescente attacco russo contro le città ucraine. Merz annuncerà un pacchetto di misure che include lo stanziamento di 1 miliardo di euro in aiuti militari e 350 milioni di euro per la riparazione delle infrastrutture energetiche, secondo quanto riferito da funzionari del governo tedesco. Si prevede inoltre che la visita finalizzi un accordo per la produzione congiunta di vari tipi di droni. "Mi sono recato oggi a Kiev perché l'Ucraina ha bisogno di tutto il nostro sostegno nelle prossime settimane", ha dichiarato Merz, affermando che le forze russe stanno bombardando città, edifici residenziali e centrali termiche. "Se non si ferma la Russia, prima o poi la sua macchina da guerra si rivolterà contro di noi". "Oggi dirò al presidente Zelenskiy che può continuare a contare sul nostro aiuto", ha aggiunto Merz. Il cancelliere tedesco è accompagnato dal Ministro dell'Economia Katherina Reiche e da una delegazione economica che comprende dirigenti di Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, DiehlDefence, Quantum Systems e altre aziende.

Onu. “400 civili uccisi in Ucraina dall'inizio dell'anno, +55% rispetto al 2025”

Nei primi otto mesi del 2026 in Ucraina si sono registrati in media oltre 400 civili uccisi o feriti ogni settimana, con un aumento del 55% rispetto allo stesso periodo del 2025. Lo ha dichiarato l'Alto Commissario delle Nazioni Unite per i Diritti Umani Volker Turk al Consiglio per i Diritti Umani a Ginevra, come riportato dal Kyiv Independent. L'ufficio di Turk ha documentato 15.280 civili uccisi o feriti nei primi otto mesi dell'anno, a seguito dell'intensificarsi degli attacchi russi contro le infrastrutture civili. Sul fronte, l'ufficio ha rilevato che quasi 2.500 civili sono stati uccisi o feriti dai bombardamenti aerei russi nello stesso periodo, il 62% in più rispetto all'anno precedente.

L'ufficio delle Nazioni Unite ha inoltre riscontrato livelli "scioccanti" di violenza sessuale contro civili e prigionieri di guerra. Turk ha accusato la Federazione Russa di utilizzare tali "atti abominevoli per torturare, intimidire e costringere individui e comunità". Secondo il Report, dei 1.004 casi accertati di violenza sessuale legata al conflitto, commessi tra febbraio 2022 e luglio 2026 contro civili e prigionieri di guerra, l'89% è stato attribuito alle forze russe. L'11% del totale dei casi accertati è stato attribuito alle forze ucraine, con minacce di violenza sessuale che rappresentano quasi la metà di queste violazioni.

A Zaporizhzhia ha aperto il primo asilo sotterraneo. Lo ha annunciato su Telegram il primo ministro ucraino Serhii Koretskyi, secondo quanto riportato da Ukrinform. "Vicino alla linea del fronte, ha aperto il primo asilo sotterraneo. Ora, 115 bambini potranno imparare, giocare e mangiare durante la giornata in un ambiente sicuro", ha dichiarato Koretskyi. Secondo il primo ministro, la struttura sotterranea - dotata di protezione dalle radiazioni e con una superficie di oltre 900 metri quadrati - è progettata per ospitare 140 persone ed è accessibile ai bambini con bisogni educativi speciali. "Insieme alle autorità locali, stiamo lavorando per creare le condizioni per un ambiente educativo sicuro a fronte della continua minaccia russa. Soprattutto nelle città e nelle comunità situate vicino al fronte", ha sottolineato. Quello di Zaporizhzhia è il secondo asilo sotterraneo aperto in Ucraina, il primo, denominato "Mobil" e progettato per accogliere 260 bambini, è entrato in funzione nella comunità di Pisochna, nella regione di Kharkiv, all'inizio dell'attuale anno scolastico.

Attacco russo contro nave cargo nel Mar Nero, un morto e tre feriti

Un marinaio è morto e altri tre membri dell'equipaggio sono rimasti feriti in un attacco russo contro una nave cargo civile battente bandiera liberiana in un porto vicino a Odessa, sul Mar Nero. Lo ha riferito l'Autorità ucraina dei porti marittimi, citata dal Kyiv Independent, precisando che la vittima era un motorista e che altri 13 membri dell'equipaggio sono stati evacuati.

items.title: In Lettonia gli exit poll danno in grande vantaggio il partito del primo ministro uscente pro Ucraina, ma buoni risultati anche per i partiti filorussi
items.content:
Alle elezioni parlamentari in Lettonia gli exit poll danno in grande vantaggio Lista Unita, il partito del primo ministro uscente di centrodestra Andris Kulbergs, in una misura sorprendente: per gli exit poll Lista Unita sarebbe oltre il 35 per cento, mentre i sondaggi lo davano intorno al 23. Gli exit poll danno poi intorno all’11 per cento entrambi i partiti filorussi, Prima la Lettonia e Potenza Sovrana, che hanno molto aumentato i consensi rispetto alle ultime elezioni del 2022 (il primo aveva preso il 6,3 per cento, il secondo il 3,3).

I rapporti del paese con la Russia d’altra parte sono stati uno dei temi centrali di queste elezioni: i partiti filorussi hanno approfittato dei problemi dell’economia lettone e del sistema sanitario per sostenere che il paese debba tornare ad avere rapporti più stretti con la Russia e interrompere il sostegno all’Ucraina nella guerra contro la Russia, per investire quei soldi in altro modo. La Lettonia è un membro dell’Unione Europea e della NATO, e in più confina con Russia e Bielorussia: l’invasione russa dell’Ucraina è una questione di sicurezza interna assai più che in altri paesi. Kulbergs è un convinto sostenitore dell’Ucraina e ha già escluso qualsiasi alleanza con i partiti filorussi per governare. L’affluenza è stata la più bassa di sempre per elezioni parlamentari, di poco superiore al 50 per cento.

items.title: Reasons I didn't become an EMT, ranked
items.summary: Article URL: https://ben.stolovitz.com/posts/reasons-not-emt-ranked/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49947631 Points: 145 # Comments: 71
items.content:
My main job is software engineering, but I’ve always been interested in medicine. A friend turned me onto the idea in college, and it rattled around my head for years. I delayed for a long time — until finally, in 2024, I took a month off and got my EMT.

Here are actual reasons I delayed getting my license , sorted loosely by ridiculousness:

Yes; my accelerated class ( NOLS Wilderness EMT ) took 28 consecutive days. I was only able to take the class because Microsoft switched to unlimited vacation, my boss was great, and I had the money to fly to Wyoming for the course (the usual alternative is a semester of night school!). And to be a good EMT, you have to actually take calls on an ambulance, hopefully more than the typical “1 weekend a month” minimum.

Yes. This was a huge barrier: I had an awful experience with some first responders a few years after college — bad enough that I gave up on getting my EMT for a while.

There are a lot of burned-out people in EMS . Many services — including the one I saw — are incredibly fratty, to be charitable. Lord help you if you are a woman . You will hear many excuses for these issues, but, yes, culture is a huge concern.

This is similar to culture, but a bit more silly. Yes, first responders tend to be a tight-knit, hereditary community. NYC firefighters, for example, often come from big firefighter families. But first responders (especially volunteers!) also come from all backgrounds — the person who onboarded me into my current position is a PM at another tech company.

So maybe EMTs were ok — but what about the EMT students I would learn with? Wouldn’t they all be 18-year-old adventure junkies or jocks?

Yes, most were, and they were awesome . My course was full of enthusiastic 18-year-old pre-meds who were excited to learn, and several people my age, who wanted to learn medicine for the same reasons I did.

If you’re nervous, I think it helped that I chose a Wilderness EMT program in July . It filters to that crowd.

I would often consider studying EMS (Emergency Medical Services) when my day job wasn’t going well. And so it would always be a bit of a sign that I should refocus at work — onto more meaningful things.

While that’s a good signal, it’s alright to put energy into things beyond work. And, once I got my certificate, balancing work & EMS has been straightforward.

Yup — I never dreamed of riding on an ambulance. Some people really do. It’s their vocation. It’s not mine.

But no one forces you to step onto an ambulance once you have your EMT. You can just… know how to do CPR really well. That’s a really cool skill to have.

If you’re not an EMT, it’s not super clear what an EMT can do. On the one hand, it’s not just “driving an ambulance,” but on the other hand, you need a paramedic for most serious calls. In some sense, it kinda is “knowing how to do CPR really well.” I trained with the same AEDs any layperson uses (EMTs aren’t allowed to use manual defibrillators), but I trained many, many more times than a layperson (plus I get to use oxygen).

But, as before, the training is still pretty cool. I loved every bit of first aid training I got; EMT school was just as fun.

Kinda. Big cities tend to have all-paid staff; volunteer positions are a bit farther out. But not that much farther out: even ignoring religious services like Hatzalah in NYC, Hoboken across the water has volunteer EMS. It’s, like, one stop on the PATH. (Volunteering in Seattle or near San Francisco is more difficult).

I didn’t want to work a part-time position — then it would just be another job, and I like my current job. But volunteer jobs are straightforward enough to find, especially if you have a car.

The culture barrier was strong enough that, for a time, I was convinced never to join an ambulance company. If you’re not on an ambulance, it’s very hard to fulfill the NREMT’s continuing education requirements , so your certificate will quickly expire.

But, again, it’s OK to learn stuff without planning to use it anywhere. And isn’t continuous learning part of the point?

Again, trying to avoid ambulances, I found search and rescue. Search and rescue (SAR) is badass. A snippet from one SAR orientation packet :

If you have registered and do not show up at training that weekend, we will make every effort to locate you, and we are incredible at finding people.

But in my heart I always wanted to treat people; and when I met SAR folks, it was clear that I wouldn’t be an effective EMT without experience on a truck.

I did 😃. I read books and Reddit posts. I took CPR and Stop the Bleed classes. I took a weekend Wilderness First Aid class with NOLS (strongly recommend!).

But I still craved more. At a certain point — as I mention in How this site works —just do the real thing .

It’s expensive, and getting new credentials is an expensive hobby.

Indeed! My course cost about $5,000, not including airfare, renting a car, & taking vacation for a month. You can do this for much cheaper (a typical course is around $2,000 and does not require 28 days vacation), but $2k is still quite expensive for some fun.

But if you’ve done the cheaper stuff, if you’re still interested after so many years, if you’re excited about using your money for an experience like this… how could it possibly be a waste?

So I signed up with no real use for it! After years of delay, I started an EMT course with no plans to use it after. I was simply excited to learn.

Working on an ambulance after was basically a happy accident, where I met a crew I happened to like. But it’s always fine to learn something for its own sake.

For someone who “didn’t want to do this,” I sure spent a lot of time on Reddit reading about what the job would entail. I sure signed up for a lot of First Aid classes. I sure told a lot of people I was interested.

I will always be a software engineer: it’s just who I am. And I learned during training that full-time EMS was not for me, after watching a woman negotiate with insurance to see if they’d cover the helicopter that would save her husband’s life.

But not interested in learning this at all ? Not being able to help people; to be a source of calm when things are actually on fire? Nonsense.

EMTs do menial work. They load & unload stretchers. They fold blankets, restock, and clean ambulances. EMTs are basically the least-trained medical personnel in any emergency (ignoring the odd EMR ). They cannot diagnose; they follow fixed protocols, and they defer to better-trained personnel for anything more severe than a broken arm.

Descriptions of EMT work inadvertently make the job seem directly heroic or glamorous: waking up at 3AM to rush a heart attack patient to the ER. It is not. The bulk of the job is waiting around, doing paperwork, cleaning, and backing up narrow driveways. It is very frequently boring & aimless.

But that tedium is because you are waiting & ready to help. So it is indirectly glamorous. As an EMT, I get to put on a uniform, and, while we’re at Dunkin Donuts for coffee, wave at the kids staring at the shiny ambulance.

I worried that an EMT certificate would be basically useless: that it would not teach me everything I expected, or that I’d still need more training on the job.

Both things are true. I learned a lot, but upon stepping onto an ambulance for the first time, it was clear how much more there was to know. Every other EMT knows so much more than I do.

But that’s the most magic part of being an EMT. It opens up an entire universe of new things to learn. It is the minimum qualification you need to enter this world: to work with firefighters and paramedics and doctors and social workers and search & rescue and disaster response personnel — and to see what you want to learn next .

A similar complaint I see on Reddit is that an EMT course only really teaches how to run an ambulance. That it is not useful for anyone interested in self-reliance or general survival skills because it requires supplies & logistics only available in a full EMS system.

Not only is that demonstrably false (my Wilderness EMT certificate is specifically for scenarios where supplies are limited and evacuation is difficult), it’s also unhelpful. What alternatives are there? Become a doctor? Join the National Guard?

Again, EMT is the fastest, easiest way to become a first responder. A good EMT course teaches you to be calm & useful in terrifying situations. A good EMT job drills that in. When that’s not enough, you’ll be ready for deeper qualifications.

That was some of the most unhelpful advice I found before getting my EMT. Ignore it.

That’s the thing — you cannot learn this alone. EMS services have spent decades learning how to help people effectively, and most of that knowledge is not yet available on YouTube.

This makes the worst services fratty, full of insider knowledge that they refuse to share. But the best services become places to learn, to become the next part of a chain that goes back to the first public Freedom House ambulances in the 60’s.

There is quite a lot of medicine you can do on your own in a bunker. But there is quite a lot more that you can’t. You do that medicine the way we always have — as part of a team, working with hundreds of other people.

items.title: Surely you have ultra-wideband radios on your bins too?
items.summary: Article URL: https://sjg.io/writing/binrange-have-you-actually-put-the-bins-out/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49947472 Points: 71 # Comments: 37
items.content:
Home Assistant already knows which bins (trash cans, for the international readers) are due for collection. It can tell me it’s bin night, put the right colours on a dashboard, and send me a reminder. What it can’t tell me is whether I’ve actually done anything about it.

I’m pretty sure most folk would just set a recurring reminder on their phone. As my wife will no doubt tell you, I am not most people. Some would just remember to put the bins out, like a normal person. I’m well aware that I’ve ridiculously over-engineered this. I’m also so far from normal that six radio-equipped bins seemed like an enjoyable way to spend my evenings ;)

I had an idea a number of years ago to stick cheap Bluetooth tags on my wheelie bins and use an outdoor Bluetooth proxy to work out whether they were nearby. It was frustrating. The batteries drained quickly, the proximity readings wandered about, and the proxy was unreliable in that particular installation. I wanted to know whether a bin had moved. I mostly acquired another thing to fiddle with.

AirTags were what first got me intrigued by ultra-wideband radio, or UWB. Reading more about how it worked brought the bin idea back. Over the last few weeks it’s become BinRange : a fixed radio anchor, six little battery tags, and a Home Assistant setup that combines where the bins have been seen with when they’re due. There’s a printed enclosure, custom firmware, and wireless updates as well. All of which is a fairly substantial answer to “have you put the bins out?” :D

I leaned heavily on Codex throughout the build. Astra became available part-way through, and I was really curious to see how it would do. What I love about working with AI is how quickly I can take an idea, react to the result, give it some feedback, and have something else to try. There’s plenty to write about that in other articles. For now, back to the bins.

We have one general waste bin, one food compost bin, one garden waste bin, two recycling bins, and a glass bin. Six bins. At one house. They’re not even all on the same collection schedule. I’m grateful that the Waste Collection Schedule integration for Home Assistant scrapes the council’s schedules and keeps track of what’s due, because keeping that straight is a job in itself.

With the cheap Bluetooth tags, the way to estimate distance was RSSI - received signal strength indication. You measure how strong the received signal is and use that to guess how far away the tag might be. The trouble is that signal strength depends on far more than distance. Walls, parked cars, reflections, antenna orientation, and differences between the radios and their antennas all affect it. Even battery voltage can affect the transmit power on some hardware , depending on how the device is designed. A weaker signal could mean the bin has moved further away, or it could mean something got in the way. It’s a very imprecise way to estimate distance, which explained why my original setup was so frustrating.

UWB was interesting because it measures the time taken by radio signals to travel between devices . That gives a distance measurement without having to guess it from signal strength. It still has to get a signal through the surroundings, of course. Choosing a different radio doesn’t make parked cars disappear.

I also spent a while detoured into an academic question about how many anchors I’d need to add more dimensions to that awareness. What if I wanted to know the direction as well as the distance from a point? Or the bin’s precise location - how many fixed reference points would I need to triangulate it on a 2D plane? Totally not worth it for this job, but tangential thoughts be tangential thoughts.

For the bins, I only needed to know whether each one had moved far enough from its usual storage area to count as Out. One anchor was enough to start testing that. I used a ten-metre boundary: inside is Home, beyond it is Out, when there’s a fresh reading. It’s specific to my installation, but it meant I could start with one powered board rather than turn the garden into a positioning test range.

The first experiment used two Makerfabs ESP32-WROVER/DW3000 boards , both powered over USB. Before doing anything clever with Home Assistant, I wanted to see them measure a distance. A local web view let me separate them and watch what happened without needing a USB cable stretched between the two.

The antenna orientation made a surprisingly large difference. At about ten metres, changing the boards from flat to upright took the observed success rate from 37% to 100% in that test. A slower radio setting with a longer preamble also worked where the initial fast setting struggled. These were useful discoveries to make before designing anything around the first result.

The first time I calibrated it with a tape measure and watched the reported distance differ from my measurement by less than two centimetres, my mind was utterly blown. Two little boards were exchanging radio signals and agreeing with a tape measure to that degree.

In the later recorded test, a measured gap of 10.1 metres produced an average reading of about 10.09 metres, with a standard deviation of three centimetres. That was encouraging for a project which only needed to recognise a bin leaving a storage area. The under-two-centimetre result was what I saw in that first calibration, rather than a promise of that accuracy for every tag, orientation, or outdoor position.

The outdoor walk was more revealing. Readings were reliable to roughly thirty metres, then intermittent further out. The furthest recorded reading was 37.28 metres, with gaps. A car could block the path completely. Holding a board upright in the open and mounting a little tag beneath a bin rim were clearly going to be different tests.

The anchor publishes its readings over MQTT, and Home Assistant discovers a separate device for each tag. I considered an ESPHome component, but it wasn’t adding much to the arrangement I wanted. There’s no extra BinRange server or cloud service, and the radios can keep ranging while Home Assistant or the MQTT connection is unavailable.

The development boards were useful for proving the link. I didn’t want one hanging off every bin, with a battery and an improvised box attached. The bin-side hardware needed to be a small, self-contained puck.

I explored custom tags and commercial ones, with the important question being whether I could run my own firmware and use them with my own anchor. A small UWB tag isn’t automatically compatible with another UWB product. The packaged tags I eventually bought were KKM K4Ws, with an nRF52833 processor, a DW3110 radio and a LIS3DH accelerometer. They take removable CR2477 coin cells (which, btw, are some chonky boy coin cells! I’ve not seen them before, thems fat).

The two Makerfabs boards came to US$123.64 including shipping. Ten sample tags at US$25 each, a programming jig and shipping came to another US$330. Those are what the experiment cost at the time, rather than a current shopping list or the cost of a finished six-bin kit. I suspect I should avoid calculating a payback period.

The supplier said the tags could run my firmware and offered a jig to reach the programming connections. I was far more interested in the hardware they were supplying and knowing that programming access wasn’t locked out in some way. None of their existing software features mattered to me. Claims about battery life were meaningless for my use once I was going to be the one deciding when the CPU slept and what woke it up.

I’m pretty familiar with nRF52 devices. I’ve used them for years, going back to my time at rlab. They make brilliant little low-power microprocessors , happy to spend most of their lives asleep. If you’re clever with your scheduling and interrupts, you can drag these things out for years on a small battery in the right application. That was much more interesting to me than whatever the supplied firmware happened to do.

I used a spare Nesso device as a programming probe for the pogo-pin jig. I started with a development tag, then commissioned the packaged ones one at a time: programme it, establish its identity, pair it, label it, assign it to a bin, and put it back together. There are several identities involved, including the printed label, the chip identity, and the addresses used by the radios.

Side note: the cases the tags were supplied in had seemingly unique serial numbers printed on them, with QR codes containing those serials. Presumably they serve some purpose in the supplier’s stock firmware and software. I couldn’t find any association with the embedded devices’ MAC addresses or similar identifiers, so they were essentially useless to me. Which is a shame really - if they’d been the radio MAC addresses, for example, that would have been useful!

The manufacturer had connected the accelerometer’s interrupt output to a GPIO pin on the nRF, which is incredibly useful. It means I can let the nRF sleep for very long periods, send no radio traffic during that sleep, and wake it up when a physical event happens. Once things settle down, it returns to occasional check-ins, with the UWB radio sleeping between attempts. The firmware default is ten minutes when stationary; I’ve since changed the installed fleet to thirty minutes using controls in Home Assistant, while keeping the five-second moving reports.
